strengths: The paper identifies and clearly motivates a genuine gap between two existing paradigms (Text-to-SQL and TSQA): SQL's inability to express morphological/shape intents and TS language models' inability to scale to long histories. The problem formulation (NLQ4TSDB) is a useful and well-justified new framing.

The Search-Then-Verify design is intuitive and well-engineered: a lightweight multi-scale SAX-based symbolic index enables cheap SQL-based candidate pruning, while Python verification with a curated operator library (change-point detection, DTW, ACF, Theil-Sen slope, Pearson correlation) grounds fuzzy linguistic concepts in precise computation. This neuro-symbolic decomposition is a sensible and practical systems contribution.

NLQTSBench is a carefully constructed benchmark with a clear four-level taxonomy (basic ops, pattern recognition, semantic reasoning, insight synthesis), deterministic/auditable ground truth via controlled signal injection, and a human visual verification step to filter ambiguous cases -- a reasonable compromise between realism and label reliability.

Comprehensive experiments against both time-series-model baselines (ChatTS, ITFormer, Time-R1) on a Lite/short-context variant and Text-to-SQL baselines (MAC-SQL, Xiyan-SQL, Omni-SQL) on the full long-horizon benchmark, with consistent and often large improvements for Sonar-TS across nearly all sub-tasks.

The ablation study (removing Feature Tables, Experiences, and Verification) is informative and supports the claimed necessity of each module, particularly showing that Verification is critical for algorithmic tasks (PD, IS) and Feature Tables are critical for morphology tasks (CT).

Strong reproducibility support: extensive appendix detailing SAX computation, query templates per level, evaluation metric formulas, and full prompt templates for the planner, code generator, experience summarizer/updater.
weaknesses: The benchmark is built entirely from a single source dataset (CausalRivers) via synthetic signal injection on top of real backgrounds; despite calibration and human review, this raises concerns about domain diversity and whether findings generalize beyond river/hydrology-style signals and the specific injected primitive families used.

Queries are generated from a fixed set of parameterized templates (detailed in Appendix A.2.2) rather than collected from real users, so the benchmark's claim to reflect natural, diverse user phrasing is limited; linguistic variability of real NLQ4TSDB usage is not really tested.

An important baseline is missing: a general LLM+code agent that operates directly on raw data (via Python only, no SQL/SAX index) at the same long-horizon scale, which would help isolate whether gains stem from the 'Search' (symbolic index) component specifically versus simply having an LLM agent with code execution and retries. The 'w/o Feature Table' ablation partially covers this but the comparison is not framed as a baseline against competing systems.

Results rely on a single backbone LLM (DeepSeek-V3) with no sensitivity analysis across different backbone models, and no reported variance/multiple-run statistics, making it hard to assess robustness of the reported gains versus prompt/model-specific effects.

For Level 4 (Insight Synthesis), baseline results are entirely absent (marked '-') for all comparison methods, so the reported average score advantage for Sonar-TS partly reflects a category where no comparison was possible, slightly overstating the comprehensiveness of the 'Avg.' columns.

No analysis of computational cost, latency, or number of LLM calls/retries incurred by the multi-stage pipeline (planning, code generation, self-correction, experience update), which is relevant given the framework's intended use as an interactive querying system.

The benchmark's claimed global series length (~170K points) is comparatively modest relative to the paper's own framing of real-world TSDBs containing 'millions of points,' somewhat undercutting the claimed motivation for the scalability challenge being addressed.

SAX itself is a well-established 2007 technique; the core technical novelty lies in the orchestration/engineering of existing components (SAX index + LLM planning + code generation + experience loop) rather than a fundamentally new algorithmic contribution, which somewhat limits originality.

strengths: The paper targets an underexplored and practically relevant gap: neither Text-to-SQL nor context-limited time series QA models can handle morphology-driven queries over massive, unsegmented TSDB histories, and this framing is clearly motivated.

The four-level task taxonomy (Basic Operations, Pattern Recognition, Semantic Reasoning, Insight Synthesis) is a sensible organizing structure for evaluating NLQ4TSDB capabilities at increasing complexity.

The Search-Then-Verify design (SQL over multi-scale SAX/statistical feature tables for candidate pruning, followed by Python-based algorithmic verification) is an intuitive and reasonably well-engineered neuro-symbolic architecture, with a concrete library of verification operators (ACF, DTW, PELT, Theil-Sen, Pearson correlation).
The ablation study (Table 2) clearly isolates the contribution of feature tables, experiences, and verification, showing plausible and interpretable degradation patterns.
Extensive appendix detailing prompts, SAX construction, operator signatures, and the data synthesis pipeline supports partial reproducibility of the described system.
weaknesses: Significant risk of circularity between benchmark construction and the proposed method: ground-truth patterns for Levels 2-4 are injected using parametric primitives (Gaussian spikes, sigmoid boxes, composite sinusoids) and labeled via algorithms (PELT change-points, ACF periodicity, Theil-Sen slope) that are essentially the same primitives packaged into Sonar-TS's verification operator library. This gives Sonar-TS a strong built-in advantage that is not available to baselines and calls into question whether the large performance gap reflects genuine methodological superiority or benchmark-method alignment.

Baseline comparisons appear unfair/mismatched: Text-to-SQL systems (MAC-SQL, Xiyan-SQL, Omni-SQL) have no code-execution or verification capability at all, and time series models (ChatTS, ITFormer, Time-R1) are evaluated only on a cropped 512-point 'Lite' subset by design. There is no baseline that combines an LLM with code-execution/operator access but without Sonar-TS's specific offline indexing, so the paper cannot cleanly attribute gains to the proposed pipeline versus simply having access to Python execution and domain operators.

The benchmark is built on a single real-world dataset (CausalRivers, hydrology domain) with only 831 queries, despite the introduction motivating the problem with IoT, financial trading, and AIOps use cases; no cross-domain evaluation is provided to support claims of general applicability.

The paper repeatedly claims to be the 'first systematic study' and 'first large-scale benchmark' for this setting, which somewhat overstates novelty given existing TSQA benchmarks (Time-MQA, QuAnTS, MTBench) already address related reasoning tasks; the primary novel axis is context length/scale rather than task types, and this distinction is not sufficiently substantiated with broader empirical scope.

Level 4 Insight Synthesis evaluation relies on a composite score with manually chosen weights (0.4/0.3/0.2/0.1) described only as 'experimental calibration,' without justification, sensitivity analysis, or validation that these weights correlate with human judgment of report quality.

No code, data, or benchmark release is mentioned/linked, and no information is given about annotator count, agreement statistics, or inter-rater reliability for the 'human visual verification' step, limiting reproducibility and trust in benchmark quality.

Only a single LLM backbone (DeepSeek-V3) is evaluated for Sonar-TS; there is no analysis of robustness across different backbone models, nor any reporting of latency/cost, despite the paper's central claim of resolving 'computational infeasibility' of full-history scanning.
No variance/statistical significance reporting across runs, which is important given the framework's reliance on LLM sampling, retries, and stochastic experience accumulation.

strengths: Clearly motivates and formalizes a novel, practically relevant task (NLQ4TSDB) that sits at the underexplored intersection of Text-to-SQL and time-series QA, with a crisp problem formulation (Eq. 1-2).

NLQTSBench is a thoughtfully designed hierarchical benchmark (4 levels, 9 sub-tasks) that meaningfully differs from prior short-context TSQA benchmarks by requiring long-horizon evidence localization (~11K point windows, 170K+ point histories).

The data construction pipeline (template formulation + controlled signal injection + human visual verification) is well documented in the appendix and provides auditable, SNR-calibrated ground truth, addressing the tension between realism and label reliability.

The Search-Then-Verify architecture is a sensible and interpretable neuro-symbolic design; the SAX-based feature index as a 'symbolic search handle' for regex-based morphological querying is a nice practical trick that is well explained.

Comprehensive ablations (Table 2) convincingly isolate the contribution of feature tables, experience accumulation, and the verification stage, with plausible explanations tied to specific task types (e.g., verification collapse on algorithmic tasks like PD/IS).

High level of implementation transparency (Appendix B): concrete operator library, full prompt templates for planner/generator/summarizer/updater, and SAX parameterization, which aids reproducibility.
weaknesses: The benchmark's 'real-world' time series all derive from a single background dataset (CausalRivers, hydrology domain) with synthetically injected patterns; despite the injection strategy, this raises concerns about domain diversity and generalizability of conclusions across other TSDB application domains (IoT, finance, AIOps) that motivate the paper.

The comparison against Text-to-SQL baselines (MAC-SQL, Xiyan-SQL, Omni-SQL) may be somewhat unfair/uninformative: it is unclear whether these baselines were given access to the same multi-scale feature tables and SAX index that Sonar-TS relies on, or only the raw schema — if the latter, the large performance gap partly reflects the added index rather than the search-then-verify mechanism per se. An ablation giving baselines equal access to feature tables, or a baseline using an LLM/Python agent directly on raw data (without SQL), would better isolate the contribution.

Only one backbone LLM (DeepSeek-V3) is evaluated; there is no sensitivity analysis to backbone choice, so it is unclear how much of the improvement is attributable to the framework versus this specific strong model's code-generation/planning capability.

The Level-4 'Insight Synthesis' evaluation depends on a rigid controlled-vocabulary output format and structure-aware parsing (Composite Report Score), which, while enabling deterministic scoring, somewhat departs from realistic free-form natural language report generation and may overstate reliability of the metric.

The paper provides limited discussion of runtime cost/latency and failure modes at scale (only a single qualitative case study in Fig. 4); given the multi-step LLM planning + retry loop (up to 3 retries) architecture, efficiency and cost trade-offs relative to baselines are not analyzed, which is relevant for a system framed as practical DB tooling.

The self-improving 'Experience' mechanism introduces several design choices (reward function, size cap of 20, summarize/merge/discard policy) that are not ablated for sensitivity, leaving unclear how robust results are to these hyperparameters.

Benchmark scale (831 queries) is modest relative to the claim of being 'the first large-scale benchmark,' and per-subtask counts (e.g., 78-80 for several Level 2/3 categories) may limit statistical robustness of reported differences.

strengths: The paper identifies and formally defines a genuinely underexplored problem (NLQ4TSDB) at the intersection of Text-to-SQL and TSQA, with a clear articulation (C1-C3) of why existing paradigms fall short: SQL's lack of morphological primitives, model context limits, and the fuzzy-to-precise semantic grounding gap.

NLQTSBench is a substantial and carefully engineered benchmark: it spans four complexity levels (basic ops, pattern recognition, semantic reasoning, insight synthesis), uses a principled synthetic-injection pipeline with SNR calibration to keep injected patterns both salient and distributionally consistent with real backgrounds, and includes a human visual verification stage plus task-appropriate metrics (IoU, relative accuracy, set F1, composite report score).

The Search-Then-Verify architecture is well-motivated and its components are individually justified; the ablation study convincingly demonstrates that Feature Tables, Verification, and Experiences each play distinct, largely non-redundant roles, with Verification's ablation causing near-total collapse, supporting the core design claim.

Experiments are comprehensive beyond the main comparison: parameter sensitivity (LLM backbone, SAX alphabet size), internal search-stage recall/precision analysis, and system overhead (latency, token cost, storage) versus a comparable multi-agent Text-to-SQL baseline are all reported, lending credibility to the practical claims.

The paper is transparent about limitations (synthetic data realism, SAX information loss, static Experience cap) rather than hiding them, and provides extensive appendix detail (prompts, construction pipeline, formulas) that supports reproducibility.
weaknesses: Because ground truth is entirely constructed via synthetic pattern injection onto real backgrounds, the benchmark's queries and 'events' are templated and mathematically defined; this may not reflect the diversity, ambiguity, or compositionality of authentic user queries or naturally occurring events, and the large margin over baselines could partly reflect that Sonar-TS's operator library (e.g., PELT changepoints, Theil-Sen slope) is essentially hand-tuned to match the same primitives used to generate the ground truth (Gaussian spikes, dual-sigmoid plateaus, sinusoidal oscillations), raising concern about circularity between data generation and verification operators.

The comparison baselines (generic Text-to-SQL systems, short-context TSQA models) were never designed for this long-horizon, morphology-aware task, so the 'large margin' improvement is somewhat expected and less informative about the specific merits of the Search-Then-Verify design versus, e.g., a simpler LLM agent with raw-data code-execution access (which is partially covered by the 'w/o Feature Tables' ablation, but not as a fully independent baseline in the main table).

The internal Search-stage recall is moderate (0.47-0.55 for SI/CT), yet final task accuracy is reported much lower for SI (0.33) but end-to-end numbers for other tasks are very high (e.g., PD 0.86, SM 0.94); the relationship between search recall and downstream accuracy is not fully reconciled or discussed, leaving some opacity about failure attribution across the pipeline.

The composite Insight Synthesis metric (weighted combination of trend/interval/adjective/outlier sub-scores) is somewhat ad hoc, and its weight calibration is not empirically justified beyond a qualitative claim of prioritizing trend structure.
Human verification details (number of annotators, inter-annotator agreement, rejection rate) are not reported, limiting assessment of benchmark label quality/reliability.

The framework itself is architecturally a fairly conventional LLM-agent pattern (plan -> generate SQL+code -> execute -> self-correct, plus a distilled experience memory), so the core technical novelty lies more in the domain-specific instantiation (SAX-based feature tables, time-series operator library) than in a fundamentally new algorithmic contribution.

strengths: The paper identifies a well-motivated and genuinely underexplored problem (NLQ4TSDB) at the intersection of Text-to-SQL, TSQA, and time-series similarity search, and gives a clear formalization (Eq. 1-2) along with a crisp articulation of the three core challenges (representation gap, context scale limit, semantic grounding conflict).

The proposed Search-Then-Verify framework is a sensible and interpretable neuro-symbolic design that decouples cheap symbolic pruning (SAX + SQL) from expensive but exact verification (Python operators), and the paper provides a reasonably detailed execution-complexity analysis (Sec 5.5) showing decoupling from raw series length N.

Extensive supplementary analysis: ablations isolating each component's contribution (Table 5), sensitivity to backbone size and SAX alphabet size (Appendix C.1), internal search-stage recall analysis (Appendix C.2), and system overhead comparison (Appendix C.3) — this thoroughness supports reproducibility and understanding of failure modes.

The benchmark construction pipeline (parametric injection with SNR calibration plus human visual verification) is methodologically transparent and documented in detail, and the hierarchical 4-level taxonomy is a reasonable organizing principle for future benchmark development.
Honest and specific limitations section (Appendix D) that candidly acknowledges the synthetic nature of the data, SAX information loss, and the non-scalable nature of the fixed Experience cap.
weaknesses: Severe circularity risk in the evaluation: the benchmark's ground-truth patterns are synthesized using explicit parametric primitives (Gaussian spikes, dual-sigmoid plateaus, composite sinusoids; Eqs. 4-6), while Sonar-TS's verification operator library (Table 3: PELT changepoints, Theil-Sen slope, ACF period detection) is composed of classical algorithms that are almost tailor-matched to detect exactly these primitive families. This raises serious doubt about whether the reported gains reflect general capability on real, messy morphological patterns rather than an artifact of aligned benchmark/method design choices — a significant soundness concern given that no real-world (non-injected) evaluation is provided.

Absolute performance remains modest and search-stage recall is low (0.47-0.55 for SI/CT, Table 10), meaning roughly half of true morphological targets are missed by the SQL search stage before verification even runs; overall average score is only 0.61 (and 0.30 on the Lite variant), which undercuts the framing that Sonar-TS 'effectively navigates complex temporal queries' — the paper's narrative of success is not fully consistent with the underlying numbers.

Baseline comparisons are structurally imbalanced: Text-to-SQL baselines (MAC-SQL, Xiyan-SQL, Omni-SQL) are not given access to the same multi-scale SAX/feature-table index that Sonar-TS relies on, so the 'large margin' improvements on morphology tasks partly reflect access to auxiliary infrastructure rather than purely better reasoning; a fairer ablation would equip baselines with the same feature tables to isolate the LLM-orchestration contribution.

Claims of scale ('massive TSDB-scale histories... often millions of points') are not matched by the actual experimental setup, where the average search space per query is only ~12k points (Table 2) and even Level-3 tasks average ~30k points — this is a much smaller regime than the motivating examples in the Introduction, making the 'scalability' claim only partially substantiated.

No statistical significance testing or variance/error bars are reported across runs, and the primary results rely on a single proprietary backbone (DeepSeek-V3); reproducibility is further limited because full API-based LLM behavior can drift over time despite code release.

The Text-to-SQL baselines score near zero on most tasks by design (SQL structurally cannot express morphological predicates), which is unsurprising and somewhat diminishes the informativeness of the 'large margin' comparison — a more interesting comparison would include stronger LLM-agent baselines equipped with code-execution capability but without the SAX index, to isolate the contribution of the symbolic index versus general agentic reasoning.

strengths: Clearly motivates and formalizes a genuinely underexplored problem (NLQ4TSDB), providing a well-argued gap analysis against Text-to-SQL, TSQA, and time series similarity search paradigms, including a clean capability comparison table (MP/MS/NLG).

The proposed Search-Then-Verify framework is a sensible and well-engineered neuro-symbolic design: SQL search over multi-scale SAX-based feature tables for coarse candidate pruning, followed by Python-based operator verification for exact grounding. The design decouples cost from raw series length, which is important for TSDB-scale querying.

NLQTSBench is a substantial and carefully constructed benchmark (1,153 queries, four-level taxonomy, ~12k average context length) with a principled data construction pipeline (parametric primitive injection, SNR calibration to keep injections realistic relative to background noise, and human visual verification), addressing the real bottleneck of ground-truth annotation for morphological queries.

Experimental evaluation is thorough: main comparison against both TSQA and Text-to-SQL baselines, a comprehensive ablation isolating the contribution of Feature Tables, Experiences, Verification, and Self-Correction, plus additional studies on backbone sensitivity, SAX alphabet size, intermediate search recall, and system overhead.

High reproducibility effort: detailed appendices with prompt templates, hyperparameters, SAX construction formulas, query templates, and evaluation metric definitions per task type; code release is mentioned.

The ablation results are informative and support the necessity of each architectural component (e.g., near-total collapse without Verification, large morphology-task drops without Feature Tables), providing good evidence for the paper's core design claims.
weaknesses: The benchmark ground truth relies entirely on synthetically injected patterns overlaid on real backgrounds rather than authentic user queries and organically occurring events; the authors acknowledge this limitation, but it raises concerns about whether reported results generalize to real, messier, non-templated queries and noisier real-world morphology.

The core symbolic representation (SAX) is a well-known 2007 technique with inherent quantization/information loss, and the reported intermediate Search-stage recall is modest (0.47–0.55 for Composite Trend/Shape Identification), suggesting the search stage frequently misses true candidates; it is unclear how much of the reported end-to-end accuracy is aided by templated query structure that happens to align well with SAX regex patterns versus genuine morphological robustness.

Baseline selection is somewhat limited/dated relative to the fast-moving Text-to-SQL and TSQA literature (e.g., no code-interpreter-augmented or agentic long-context TS-LLM baselines), and all baselines are evaluated only on the authors' own newly introduced benchmark, so comparisons cannot be cross-checked against external, established test suites.

The framework depends heavily on a hand-curated, capacity-sensitive prompting/Experience mechanism (hard-capped at 20 items, requires a hold-out profiling set); sensitivity to backbone size is significant (Avg. score drops from 0.61 with DeepSeek-V3 to 0.36 with Qwen3.5-9B), raising concerns about robustness and practicality when smaller/local LLMs are required for privacy-sensitive deployments (which the paper's own Impact Statement flags as a target use case).

The Level 4 composite report score is an ad hoc weighted combination of four sub-scores with manually calibrated weights, and no inter-annotator agreement or variance/uncertainty (e.g., multiple runs, confidence intervals) is reported for any of the main results, making it hard to assess the statistical robustness of the large performance gaps claimed.

No real-world case study or deployment validation beyond the synthetic benchmark is provided, so the practical significance of the reported gains for actual TSDB operators/analysts remains unverified.
